LAB_04 — IDS/IPS Deployment, Configuration, and Validation: what you do, step by step

This page shows every step of the full LAB_04 guide as a short animation: the command as it is typed, the answer the screen gives, and what to keep as evidence. Press Play from the start under a drawing to watch it; the still picture is the final state. Every command has a Copy button; the check marks at the top count your progress and stay in this browser only.

The animations are drawn re-creations of what the screen shows, not recordings: version numbers, counts, ports and timestamps are examples, and the version note under a drawing says what may look different on your machine.

Before you start names, addresses, the sensor machine and its adapters

The company is NorthMaple Accounting Inc. in the manual; the Class 7–8 pages and their RLE files call the same company "Laurentide Outfitters inc." (the manual, § 1.2, permits renaming) — keep the name of your Chapters 1 to 3. The drawings use the lecture addresses so that the provided files work unchanged; if your LAB_01 zoning differs, use your own values in HOME_NET, the rules and the tests.

The sensor machine, ids-01: one new Linux VM (Virtual Machine) — Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (Long-Term Support) or newer; 2 processors, 2 GB of memory (4 GB recommended), 20 GB of disk; adapter 1 on NAT, adapter 2 on the lab network in promiscuous mode. Pre-flight: ping -c 2 10.10.10.20 from lab-client must answer. If your zones are separate networks with no router yet (the firewall arrives in LAB_05), put the three lab machines and adapter 2 of ids-01 on one internal network for this lab and say so in your chapter.

Cloud (AWS, Azure) and CyberQuébec pod: there is no promiscuous mode to set — install the sensor on web-01 itself, on its own interface; every test still produces its alert. Skip the two VirtualBox drawings and start at step 2 with the interface name that ip -br link shows.

Before you start — the sensor machine and its second network adapter

Version note (September 2026). Simplified drawing of VirtualBox 7.2. In 7.1 and 7.2 the Advanced block appears in Expert mode (toggle at the top right); in 7.0 every option is always visible. In the cloud (AWS, Azure) and on a CyberQuébec pod this setting does not exist — see the cloud note above.

Do

  • VirtualBox → ids-01 → Settings → Network.
  • Adapter 1: Attached to NAT (Network Address Translation) — Internet for packages and rules.
  • Adapter 2: Enable Network Adapter → Attached to: Internal Network (or the host-only network that carries the lab-client ↔ web-01 traffic) → Name: the same network as your lab machines → Advanced → Promiscuous Mode: Allow All → OK.

See

Promiscuous mode makes the adapter pass every frame on the wire to the sensor, not only the frames addressed to itself. Without it, the counter of step 8 stays at zero.

Keep as evidence

Nothing yet — the environment page of step 8 will record the VM name, interface and adapters.

Part 1 — Deployment (Class 7) steps 1 to 8, about 30 minutes; commands are typed in a terminal on ids-01, sudo runs a command with administrator rights

1

Snapshot first

Version note (September 2026). Snapshots tool of the VirtualBox Manager 7.x. While the VM is running, the VM window's menu Machine ▸ Take Snapshot… (Host+T) does the same; VirtualBox 6.1 shows the same list behind the Snapshots toolbar icon.

Do

  • VirtualBox Manager → select ids-01 → Snapshots → Take → Snapshot Name: LAB_04-before-install → OK.

See

The snapshot appears above Current State. A mistake in the next steps then costs one click (Restore).

Keep as evidence

Nothing — but repeat a snapshot before any large edit.

2

Find the monitoring interface name

Version note (September 2026). Names such as enp0s3 and enp0s8 come from the adapter position in VirtualBox. On other virtualization software (VMware, Proxmox, cloud) the names are ens33, ens5, eth1 or similar — the rule is the same: the adapter that is not the Internet one.

Do

  1. ip -br link
  2. sudo ip link set enp0s8 up
  3. ip -br link

See

Two names besides lo: enp0s3 (adapter 1, NAT) and enp0s8 (adapter 2, the lab network). The guide writes enp0s8; replace it with yours everywhere. After the second command the state reads UP.

Keep as evidence

Nothing yet.

3

Install the sensor — Suricata 8.x (Option A)

Version note (September 2026). Ubuntu 24.04 LTS shown (the lines say noble); on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS the code name in the lines differs, the commands do not. 8.0.x: the third number changes with every maintenance release. Without the OISF (Open Information Security Foundation) repository, Ubuntu 24.04 installs 7.0.x, which is accepted. If add-apt-repository reports no packages for your Ubuntu release, use the plain sudo apt install -y suricata jq curl or the official install page. Debian: sudo apt install -y suricata jq curl; Rocky/AlmaLinux: sudo dnf install -y epel-release && sudo dnf install -y suricata jq curl. Option B, Snort 3: apt show snort — only a 3.x package is usable (Ubuntu's own package may still be 2.9.x); otherwise follow docs.snort.org. The Snort 3 variants of the next steps are in the full guide.

Do

  1. sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y software-properties-common
  2. sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:oisf/suricata-stable
  3. sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y suricata jq curl
  4. suricata -V
  5. sudo systemctl stop suricata

See

suricata -V answers This is Suricata version 8.0.x RELEASE. The last command stops the service the package started, so that only one engine opens the interface tonight.

Keep as evidence

A screenshot of the suricata -V line (goes into the environment page).

4

Set HOME_NET — the setting beginners get wrong

Version note (September 2026). nano 7.2 (Ubuntu 24.04); nano 8.x (Ubuntu 26.04) shows the same shortcuts. The line numbers (19 and 25 here) depend on the version of suricata.yaml that came with your package. Snort 3: the same values go into snort.lua as HOME_NET = '[…]' and EXTERNAL_NET = '!$HOME_NET'.

Do

  1. sudo nano /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
  2.     HOME_NET: "[10.10.10.0/24,20.20.10.0/24,20.20.20.0/24]"
    EXTERNAL_NET: "!$HOME_NET"
  3. grep -n HOME_NET /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml | head -2

See

In nano: Ctrl+W, type HOME_NET, Enter; replace the value inside the quotation marks with your three ranges, keep the four leading spaces; Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X. Rules have a direction (-> $HOME_NET = into the company), so a wrong HOME_NET makes rules silent. /24 is CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation: every address that starts with 10.10.10.

Keep as evidence

Screenshot of the grep -n HOME_NET … | head -2 output.

5

Tell the engine which interface to watch

Version note (September 2026). The af-packet block has a second entry - interface: default further down — leave it; only the first interface: line changes. Same in Suricata 7 and 8.

Do

  1. sudo nano /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
  2. af-packet:
  - interface: enp0s8

See

Ctrl+W, type af-packet:, Enter; two lines below change eth0 to your interface name; save. Tonight the interface is also given on the command line (step 7); the file value is used when the sensor later runs as a service.

Keep as evidence

Nothing.

6

Fetch a rule set now, use it tomorrow

Version note (September 2026). suricata-update 1.3.x. The download address carries your major version (…/open/suricata-8.0/…), and the rule counts change every day — yours will not match the drawing. Snort 3: download the free Snort 3 Community Rules from snort.org/downloads and unpack them into /etc/snort/rules/.

Do

  1. sudo suricata-update

See

The last lines read Writing rules to /var/lib/suricata/rules/suricata.rules: total: …; enabled: … and Done. About one minute. No Internet on ids-01? The sensor still starts, and part 2 does not need this download.

Keep as evidence

Nothing (the rule-set date goes into the environment page of step 8).

7

Test the configuration, then start the sensor in the foreground

Version note (September 2026). Suricata 7 and 8 print the short prefixes i: (info), N: (notice), W: (warning), E: (error); Suricata 6 prints a timestamp and <Notice>-style tags with the same words. W: 2 in the thread line is your number of processors. Snort 3: sudo snort -T -c /etc/snort/snort.lua, then sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.lua -i enp0s8 -A alert_fast -l /var/log/snort -k none.

Do

  1. sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -v
  2. sudo suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -i enp0s8

See

-T tests and stops: look for 0 rules failed and Configuration provided was successfully loaded. The second command runs the engine in this terminal until Ctrl+C: wait for … rules successfully loaded, 0 rules failed and Engine started. (up to a minute with ET Open). Leave this terminal open.

Keep as evidence

Screenshot of the error-free start with its rules loaded line.

8

Prove that the sensor sees traffic

Version note (September 2026). stats.log is written every 8 s (setting interval: 8 in the stats section of suricata.yaml); right after the start the file may hold fewer than three lines. Snort 3: Ctrl+C in the sensor terminal — the Packet Statistics printed at exit show the packets received.

Do

  1. ping -c 20 10.10.10.20            # on lab-client
  2. grep capture.kernel_packets /var/log/suricata/stats.log | tail -n 3      # on ids-01, second terminal

See

Open a second terminal on ids-01 (or a second SSH (Secure Shell) session). Run the grep once, generate traffic from lab-client, run it again: the last value must be larger. The counter is refreshed every 8 seconds. Counter stuck at zero: wrong interface (NAT sees only its own traffic), Promiscuous Mode at Deny, or a second engine on the interface; an allocation error at start means too little memory.

Keep as evidence

Screenshot of the counter growing during traffic, plus the environment page for chapter 4.2: VM name, interface, HOME_NET, engine version (suricata -V), rule-set date, date of the work. End of part 1.

Part 2 — Configuration and validation (Class 8) steps 9 to 15: the four rules, the six tests, the evidence

9

Add the four provided local rules

Version note (September 2026). Snort 3: same file at /etc/snort/rules/local.rules; in rules 3 and 4 write http_uri; instead of http.uri; and content:"UNION SELECT",nocase; (modifier inside the content option).

Do

  1. sudo cp RLE08-1_local.rules /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules
  2. cat /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules
  3. grep -c sid /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules

See

Four lines, one rule per line, every option closed by a semicolon. The header before the bracket (action, protocol, source, direction, destination) selects the packets; the options inside say what to look for and how to name the alert. If you type the file with sudo nano instead, copy the rules exactly from the Class 8 page. Replace the three addresses if your zones differ.

Keep as evidence

The file local.rules as loaded goes into CH4_detection/; the rule anatomy table (RLE08-1_rule-anatomy-table.csv) goes into chapter 4.3.

10a

Include the file in the configuration

Version note (September 2026). If default-rule-path above the list is /var/lib/suricata/rules, the absolute path shown here is what makes the engine find your file. Same in Suricata 7 and 8.

Do

  1. sudo nano /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
  2. rule-files:
  - suricata.rules
  - /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules

See

Ctrl+W, type rule-files:, Enter; add the new line under - suricata.rules with the same two leading spaces; save.

Keep as evidence

Nothing.

10b

Test, reload, read the count

Version note (September 2026). In Suricata 8 the suricatasc tool was rewritten but keeps the same name and command; it needs the unix socket line seen at start-up in step 7. Snort 3: sudo snort -T -c /etc/snort/snort.lua -R /etc/snort/rules/local.rules, then add -R /etc/snort/rules/local.rules to the start command.

Do

  1. sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -v
  2. sudo suricatasc -c reload-rules

See

2 rule files processed. N rules successfully loaded, 0 rules failed — N is 4 without ET Open, tens of thousands with it. A failing rule is named with its line number and reason (missing semicolon, unbalanced quotation mark, duplicated SID): fix it and test again. reload-rules reloads while the engine runs; without the socket, Ctrl+C in the sensor terminal and start it again as in step 7.

Keep as evidence

Screenshot of the rules loaded line with 0 rules failed.

11

Prepare the target (web-01)

Version note (September 2026). Python 3.12 (Ubuntu 24.04) and 3.14 (Ubuntu 26.04) print the same lines. If web-01 already runs Apache or nginx, use it as it is. Optional ET Open smoke test inside the lab — see step 11 of the full guide (rule 2100498).

Do

  1. cd ~ && sudo python3 -m http.server 80            # on web-01, only if it has no web server

See

web-01 must answer on port 80, plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): a content rule cannot read HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), whose content is encrypted. A 404 Not Found answer is fine — the rules read the request, not the answer. Leave it running during the tests.

Keep as evidence

Nothing.

12

Predict before you generate

Do

  1. sudo tail -f /var/log/suricata/fast.log            # on ids-01, second terminal

See

Open RLE08-3_validation-evidence.csv, keep the Expected column as written and empty Observed and Verdict — a prediction written after reading the log is not a prediction. Then keep this live view of fast.log open: every alert appears here the moment a rule matches.

Keep as evidence

The evidence table, to be filled row by row in step 14.

RLE08-3_validation-evidence.csv — Expected written before the run; Observed and Verdict empty until step 14
TestFrom → toActionExpectedObservedVerdict
T1lab-client → web-01ping -c 4alert sid 1000001
T2lab-client → srv-filesssh port 22alert sid 1000002

13

Generate the six tests — one action at a time, from the named machine, inside your lab only

See

curl sends one exact request; in the lab browser you may type the address instead. On Windows, ping, ssh and curl are built in (ping -n 4 instead of -c 4). Each animation below shows the client on top and the live fast.log of ids-01 below.

Keep as evidence

One cropped, captioned screenshot per test: the command as typed (client clock visible) and the matching fast.log line (same timestamp, SID, addresses).

T1 lab-client → web-01 — expected: sid 1000001

  1. ping -c 4 10.10.10.20

T2 lab-client → srv-files — expected: sid 1000002

  1. ssh -o ConnectTimeout=5 20.20.20.10

T3 lab-client → web-01 — expected: sid 1000004

  1. curl -s -o /dev/null "http://10.10.10.20/shop/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20--"

T4 lab-client → web-01 — expected: sid 1000003

  1. curl -s -o /dev/null "http://10.10.10.20/shop/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20id%20FROM%20accounts%20--"

N1 ws-admin → srv-files — expected: no alert — the one address rule 2 excludes

  1. ssh -o ConnectTimeout=5 20.20.20.10

N2 lab-client → web-01 — expected: no alert — an ordinary search

  1. curl -s -o /dev/null "http://10.10.10.20/shop/search?q=tent"
Version note (September 2026). %27, %20, %3D are the percent-encoded quotation mark, space and equals sign; the engine decodes them before comparing, so the browser form ?q=' OR 1=1 -- gives the same alert. Port numbers and timestamps in the drawings are examples. On Windows use ping -n 4. T3 and T4 are SQL (Structured Query Language) injection fragments: harmless against your own web-01, an attempt at unauthorized access under Criminal Code section 342.1 if sent to any website you do not own.
14

Observe, compare, capture

Version note (September 2026). jq 1.7 and 1.8 print the same output. Snort 3 with -A alert_fast prints the same alert line on the console.

Do

  1. sudo tail -n 200 /var/log/suricata/eve.json | jq -c 'select(.event_type=="alert") | {timestamp, sid: .alert.signature_id, src_ip, dest_ip}'
  2. sudo grep -c 1000004 /var/log/suricata/fast.log

See

Each fast.log line: timestamp, [1:1000004:2] (generator : SID : revision), message, classification, protocol, source → destination address:port. eve.json is the structured copy (JSON, JavaScript Object Notation) that jq reads. Expected equals observed → PASS; anything else — including the right SID with the wrong addresses (test run from the wrong machine) → FAIL: fix, run again, describe it in chapter 4.5.

Keep as evidence

The filled row of the evidence table for every test, plus the six screenshots.

15

When the expected alert does not appear — check in this order

Version note (September 2026). tcpdump 4.99.x — same output on every current Linux. Install it with sudo apt install -y tcpdump if the command is missing.

Do

  1. sudo tcpdump -ni enp0s8 host 10.10.10.20

See

(1) Rule loaded — start-up count or -T? (2) HOME_NET contains the addresses of the test? (3) Engine on the interface that carries the test — tcpdump shows whether the packets are visible there at all. (4) Direction and port: which machine started the connection, to which port? (5) Encryption: plain HTTP port 80, never 443. (6) Engine restarted after the last edit? (7) Test really leaving the client — a browser cache or a LAB_03 host-firewall rule can stop it; confirm with tcpdump on the client.

Keep as evidence

Whatever went wrong and how you fixed it → chapter 4.5 ("Nothing went wrong" is acceptable).

Version notes — September 2026 what this page shows, and what may look different on your machine

Ubuntu Server
24.04 LTS (Long-Term Support, supported to 2029) is what the drawings show; 26.04 LTS (April 2026) works with the same commands. Only the code name inside apt lines and the nano version differ.
Suricata
8.0.x from the OISF repository (the third number moves with each maintenance release); Ubuntu's own package on 24.04 is 7.0.x, accepted. Suricata 7 and 8 share the short log prefixes (i:, N:, W:, E:) and the same file locations; Suricata 6 prints longer, timestamped lines. suricata-update 1.3.x downloads ET Open for your major version; rule counts change daily.
Snort 3
3.x is the only accepted Snort; check with snort -V. Distribution packages may still be 2.9.x — do not use them. Rule syntax differences are marked in steps 4, 7, 9 and 10.
VirtualBox
7.2.x. The dialogs on this page are simplified drawings, not screenshots: names and positions are those of 7.1/7.2 (Basic/Expert toggle, Snapshots tool). 7.0 shows every option without the toggle; 6.1 uses the same words in slightly different places.
Cloud (AWS, Azure) and CyberQuébec pod
no promiscuous mode and no VirtualBox dialogs: install the sensor on web-01 itself, on its own interface (ip -br link shows one name such as ens5 or eth0); every test still produces its alert. On a CyberQuébec pod ask the instructor for the equivalent of the adapter setting.
Client tools
curl 8.x, OpenSSH 9.x, iputils ping: identical output on every current Linux. Windows 10/11: ping -n 4; curl and ssh are built in. jq 1.7/1.8 and tcpdump 4.99.x: same output.
Log content
timestamps, port numbers, packet counters, rule counts and the sensor's thread count in the drawings are examples; yours are different, and that is expected. What must match: the SID, the message, the direction of the addresses and 0 rules failed.

The links to every official site (Ubuntu, VirtualBox, OISF/Suricata, Snort, Emerging Threats, jq, tcpdump, curl, NIST, CIS, OWASP, MITRE, the Criminal Code) are in sections 3, 6 and 7 of the full guide. Before opening any link, check it with the VirusTotal URL (Uniform Resource Locator) scanner, as the guide asks.
